In [[mathematical logic]], the '''Scott–Curry theorem''' is a result in [[lambda calculus]] stating that if two non-empty sets of lambda terms ''A'' and ''B'' are closed under beta-convertibility then they are [[recursively inseparable]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Introduction to Combinators and (lambda) Calculus|last1=Hindley|first1=J.R.|author-link1=J. Roger Hindley|last2=Seldin|first2=J.P.|isbn=9780521268967|lccn=lc85029908|series=Cambridge Monographs on Mathematical Physics|year=1986|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]}}</ref>

==Explanation==
A set ''A'' of lambda terms is closed under beta-convertibility if for any lambda terms X and Y, if <math>X \in A</math> and X is [[Lambda calculus#Reduction|β-equivalent]] to Y then <math>Y \in A</math>. Two sets ''A'' and ''B'' of natural numbers are recursively separable if there exists a [[computable function]] <math>f : \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \{0, 1\}</math> such that <math>f(a) = 0</math> if <math>a \in A</math> and <math>f(b) = 1</math> if <math>b \in B</math>. Two sets of lambda terms are recursively separable if their corresponding sets under a [[Gödel numbering]] are recursively separable, and recursively inseparable otherwise.

The Scott–Curry theorem applies equally to sets of terms in [[combinatory logic]] with weak equality. It has parallels to [[Rice's theorem]] in computability theorem, which states that all non-trivial semantic properties of programs are undecidable.

The theorem has the immediate consequence that it is an [[undecidable problem]] to determine if two lambda terms are β-equivalent.

==Proof==
The proof is adapted from Barendregt in ''The Lambda Calculus''.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Lambda Calculus: Its Syntax and Semantics|last=Barendregt|first=H.P.|isbn=0444875085|series=Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics|volume=103|year=1985|edition=3rd|publisher=[[Elsevier Science]]}}</ref>

Let ''A'' and ''B'' be closed under beta-convertibility and let ''a'' and ''b'' be lambda term representations of elements from ''A'' and ''B'' respectively. Suppose for a contradiction that ''f'' is a lambda term representing a computable function such that <math>fx = 0</math> if <math>x \in A</math> and <math>fx = 1</math> if <math>x \in B</math> (where equality is β-equality). Then define <math>G \equiv \lambda x.\text{if}\ (\text{zero?} \ (fx)) a b</math>. Here, <math>\text{zero?}</math> is true if its argument is zero and false otherwise, and <math>\text{if}</math> is the identity so that <math>\text{if}\ b x y</math> is equal to ''x'' if ''b'' is true and ''y'' if ''b'' is false.

Then <math>x \in C \implies Gx = a</math> and similarly, <math>x \notin C \implies Gx = b</math>. By the Second Recursion Theorem, there is a term ''X'' which is equal to ''f'' applied to the Church numeral of its Gödel numbering, ''X{{'}}''. Then <math>X \in C</math> implies that <math>X = G(X') = b</math> so in fact <math>X \notin C</math>. The reverse assumption <math>X \notin C</math> gives <math>X = G(X') = a</math> so <math>X \in C</math>. Either way we arise at a contradiction, and so ''f'' cannot be a function which separates ''A'' and ''B''. Hence ''A'' and ''B'' are recursively inseparable.

==History==
[[Dana Scott]] first proved the theorem in 1963. The theorem, in a slightly less general form, was independently proven by [[Haskell Curry]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Logic from Russell to Church|last=Gabbay|first=D.M.|last2=Woods|first2=J.|isbn=9780080885476|series=Handbook of the History of Logic|year=2009|publisher=[[Elsevier Science]]}}</ref> It was published in Curry's 1969 paper "The undecidability of λK-conversion".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Curry |first1=Haskell B. |author-link1=Haskell Curry |date=1969 |title=The undecidability of λK-conversion |journal=[[Journal of Symbolic Logic]] |volume=January 1969 |pages=10–14}}</ref>
